newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-Baabaas give glimpse of All Black future.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-Baabaas give glimpse of All Black future.

text.p: LONDON, Dec 1 - England were expecting a blast from the past in their rugby international against the New Zealand Barbarians at Twickenham.
What they got instead was a look at the future in the 34-19 loss -- and they didn't like it.

England were obsessed with Jonah Lomu -- the man who had buried them in the World Cup semifinal last year -- in the build-up to the match, and every time the big man took hold of the ball the England players zeroed in on him.
They should have been looking elsewhere.
The most decisive contributions came from emerging players -- fullback Christian Cullen, flankers Andrew Blowers and Dylan Mika, and first five-eighth Carlos Spencer.

Cullen made several scintillating breaks, Blowers was ever-present in the loose and scored one of the Barbarians' tries. Mika and Spencer may have only been replacements, but they had a huge impact, with Spencer scoring a brilliant individual try that finally broke down England's resistance.
Even captain Sean Fitzpatrick was left scratching his head at the impact of the young players.
"It's amazing where they're coming from," Fitzpatrick said.
"I was talking to JK (John Kirwan) and said to him 'you wouldn't want to be a young back in New Zealand now -- you'd find it hard to get in the team'."
The Barbarians may not have been the full New Zealand test team, but they still had too much pace and power for England.

At least six first-choice players were left at home, giving players like prop Mark Allen, Blowers, second five-eighth Lee Stensness and centre Alama Ieremia a chance to show their skills at the top level.
They all came through superbly, out-playing England in all facets of the game and finishing strongly.
The embarrassment of riches has given coach John Hart a problem for the 1997 season, although it's a problem he doesn't mind having.
"It's a nice headache to have," he said.

With the growing pressures in international rugby and an increasingly crowded schedule -- including what he described as a "horror" 1997 programme -- New Zealand needed all the top players it could get, Hart said.
"With the intensity of rugby now that sort of depth is crucial," Hart told NZPA.
"What this tour was all about was to see if we could get players to show they are up to this level. I'm really pleased that we showed they are.
"It keeps the pressure on through the team, and that can only be a good thing.

"One of the success stories for New Zealand rugby this year is that they've worked for each other all year. They've supported each other, and that goes to all the guys on the bench, all they want is to see each other succeed, and that's really encouraging for me."
Hart said the pressures of Super 12, NPC and tests would still take its toll on players.
"There's still a question mark, because Super 12 was only in its first year," he added.
"But I believe Australia are showing that pressure with their injury rate now, and we have a horror schedule next year."
Auckland first five-eighth Spencer was one of the biggest success stories of the short Barbarians tour, which he rounded off with an ultimately match-winning try yesterday.

With four minutes to play, Spencer picked up the ball from a ruck, dummied inside then accelerated into a gap, stepped off his right foot past England halfback Andy Gomarsall and outpaced fullback Tim Stimpson in a 30-metre run to the tryline.
"It was a great moment when it opened up for me," Spencer told NZPA.
"John (Hart) told me before the game I would be going out in the second half, and I was just so keen to get out there.
"I just picked up and looked for Alama (Ieremia), but he was marked so I had to run, then there was a little gap and I went for it, managed to get past one of their guys and the line opened up.
"I wanted to have a good game to finish off the year.
"I guess it's a bit of a dream finish, and gives me a push into next season."
